column1: If i go to resolution 768x1024 is it normal for the navbar to disappear completely
No, that is not normal behavior. A sticky navigation bar should remain visible at the top of the viewport regardless of screen resolution.
The reason your .navbar disappears when resizing to a portrait aspect ratio like 768x1024 is caused by the interaction between two specific CSS properties in your SCSS:
Pulling #welcome-text up by -85px causes it to overlap directly on top of the .navbar.

While .navbar has z-index: 100, because .navbar uses position: sticky, its stacking context behaves differently when scrolling or resizing on taller aspect ratios (like 1024px vertical height). As the page recalculates dimensions, #welcome-text is being rendered on top of the navbar, hiding it completely under a background box or text element.

Remove margin-top: -85px from #welcome-text and rely on display: flex alignment instead. Since #welcome-text sits below a sticky header, setting its height to calc(100vh - 85px) naturally fills the rest of the screen without needing negative margins.

When position: sticky stops working completely upon scrolling, it is almost always caused by an ancestor container clipping the sticky element's scroll context.
In your SCSS code, there are two distinct properties causing this behavior:
Cause 1: overflow-x: hidden on body / html
Earlier we added overflow-x: hidden to prevent side-scrolling. Setting any overflow property (even just overflow-x) on a parent container breaks position: sticky in modern browsers.
The browser treats any container with non-visible overflow as a scroll container, which disconnects the element from scrolling relative to the main viewport window.
Fix: Move overflow handling to an inner wrapper instead of body / html

Remove overflow-x: hidden from html and body. If you need to stop elements from breaking layout bounds horizontally, clip individual sections or apply overflow-x: clip (which preserves stickiness in modern browsers):

This Webpack module resolution error means Webpack is searching for the file at /Users/gabeschwarz/CS409/CS409-MP1/assets/Monkey.mp4, but it cannot find a file at that exact path.
There are three common reasons for this error:
Cause 1: Incorrect Relative Path from src/
Your current code attempts to resolve ../assets/Monkey.mp4 relative to /Users/gabeschwarz/CS409/CS409-MP1/src. Moving up one level (..) looks inside the project root for an assets/ folder.
Check your file directory structure in VS Code / Terminal:
Change the path in your file to use ./assets/Monkey.mp4 (one dot):

Keep ../assets/Monkey.mp4, but double-check that the folder name is strictly lowercase (assets) and matches exact casing.
If the file extension or name is cased differently:
Ensure the filename matches case sensitivity (e.g., monkey.mp4 vs Monkey.mp4 or .MP4 vs .mp4).
Cause 2: Referencing the Path inside HTML (HtmlWebpackPlugin)
If you are using HtmlWebpackPlugin or raw HTML loading, Webpack parses <source src="..."> tags as module imports.
If your assets folder sits in public/ or dist/ rather than being bundled by Webpack, import the asset directly via JavaScript or require it:
Option A: Import in JavaScript / Component
// Set src dynamically or via template bindings
Option B: Inline Require in HTML (if using EJS/HTML templates)
Cause 3: Missing Webpack Asset Module Rule (Webpack 5)
If Webpack finds the file but still fails during compilation, your webpack.config.js may be missing a rule to process .mp4 media assets.
Add this rule under module.rules in your webpack.config.js:
type: 'asset/resource', // Asset modules natively handle media files in Webpack 5
